domain: Historical Sociology / Religious Studies / Political Economy
topic_summary: Analysis of the Protestant Reformation (1517-1648) as a composite event exhibiting simultaneous climb, drop, swap, and emergence patterns. The research context frames this as a test case for whether a single kernel with contested readings can accommodate structural overdetermination, or whether the event resists kernel decomposition entirely due to multiple independent causal chains converging without shared substrate.

key_entities: Holy Roman Empire (political container, Charles V)
Treaty of Westphalia 1648 (terminal boundary, cuius regio principle)
key_tensions: Doctrinal unity vs denominational fragmentation (reformers could not agree on fundamentals despite shared opposition)
Religious reform vs political opportunism (rulers weaponized theology for territorial control)
Scriptural authority vs papal authority (swap of legitimation source)
Centralized church governance vs local autonomy (Luther's princely model vs Calvin's presbyterian model)
Theological purity vs survival pragmatism (Anabaptist persecution, cuius regio compromises)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: NOT A SINGLE KERNEL. The Reformation exhibits structural overdetermination: multiple independent causal chains (theological dissent, printing technology, mercantile interests, nationalist fragmentation, anticlerical sentiment) converge without a shared commitment substrate that all parties read differently. The event is composite rather than contested.
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Multiple competing authority structures emerge simultaneously: scriptural literalism (Luther), institutional presbyterianism (Calvin), princely supremacy (Henry VIII), radical congregationalism (Anabaptists). No single interpretive framework adjudicates legitimacy across all variants.
commitment_system_recognition.collapse_analysis: Initial hypothesis: Reformation as contested kernel with readings (papal_continuity, scriptural_primacy, radical_autonomy). Collapse detected: these are not different readings of one shared commitment but structurally independent movements with different beneficiaries, victims, and causal mechanisms. Luther's sola scriptura and Calvin's institutional presbyterianism do not interpret the same kernel—they instantiate different authority structures from different starting points. The Anabaptist rejection of infant baptism is orthogonal to both. Temporal ambiguity (1400-1750 vs 1517-1648 vs 1517-1685) signals absence of event-kernel boundary. Reformers' inability to achieve doctrinal unity despite shared opposition to Rome confirms: no shared substrate exists to be read differently. The Reformation is a composite of overlapping but structurally independent constraint transformations, not a single kernel with contested readings.

omegas.description: The Reformation resists kernel decomposition because it is overdetermined: multiple independent causal chains (technological, theological, political, economic) converge without a shared commitment substrate. Luther's scriptural primacy, Calvin's institutional presbyterianism, and Anabaptist congregationalism are not different readings of one kernel but structurally independent movements. The inability of reformers to achieve doctrinal unity despite shared opposition confirms absence of shared substrate. This is a composite event, not a contested kernel.
omegas.source: §1.3-K kernel/reading test; collapse analysis in commitment_system_recognition

omegas.description: Temporal ambiguity (1400-1750 vs 1517-1648 vs 1517-1685) signals absence of event-kernel boundary. If the Reformation has no agreed start/end dates, it may be a historiographic construct rather than a discrete structural transformation. The 1517-1648 framing privileges Luther and Westphalia but obscures earlier dissent (Hus, Wycliffe) and later consolidation (Edict of Nantes revocation 1685).
omegas.source: Extraction phase temporal ambiguity; Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory)

omegas.description: Research context notes 'currents of nationalism, mercantilism, anticlericalism' beginning in late 14th century. These may constitute independent axes (mercantile_interest_alignment, anticlerical_sentiment) with their own epsilon values, deferred due to insufficient observables in provided research. If mercantile interests drove Reformation adoption independently of theology, the scriptural_authority_swap axis may misattribute causation.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan); extraction phase mechanism identification

omegas.description: Research states Thirty Years' War 'informed, though did not cause' by Protestant-Catholic tensions. If religious conflict was pretext rather than cause (political rivalry primary), then denominational_fragmentation may be downstream of cuius_regio_extraction rather than upstream. Causal arrow direction uncertain; affects constraint graph topology.
omegas.source: Extraction phase tension identification; §3 independence testing edge ambiguity

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: printing_press_diffusion classified as mountain (technological constraint) but may be piton (policy choice to not suppress printing). Catholic Church had capacity to ban vernacular Bibles (Index Librorum Prohibitorum) but enforcement varied by region. If suppression was feasible but not executed, the axis is a rope of institutional choice rather than a mountain of technological inevitability. Generated omega_composite_not_kernel to document kernel decomposition failure. Generated omega_mercantile_anticlerical_substrate to flag under-extraction of economic causal chains.
